channel.name: NeuralBytes
channel.description: Clear, practical explainers on machine learning and AI - from perceptrons to modern LLMs. New deep dives every month.

videos.title: A Brief History of Neural Networks

chunks.text: Welcome to NeuralBytes. Today we trace the history of neural networks, from a room-sized machine in the 1950s to the models writing poetry today.
It starts in 1958 with Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron, a single artificial neuron that learned to classify simple images by adjusting its weights.
In 1969 Minsky and Papert proved a single perceptron cannot solve the XOR problem. Funding dried up, and the field entered what we now call the first AI winter.
The thaw came in 1986, when Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularized backpropagation, showing multi-layer networks could learn internal representations.
Expert systems overpromised in the late 80s and a second AI winter followed. Neural nets survived in a few stubborn labs in Canada.
Everything changed in 2012: AlexNet, trained on GPUs, crushed the ImageNet competition and cut the error rate nearly in half. Deep learning was suddenly everywhere.
Since then the story has been scale: more data, more compute, bigger models - leading directly to the large language models we cover elsewhere on this channel.
How does a neural network actually learn? In this video we walk through backpropagation step by step, with no hand-waving.
First, the forward pass: inputs flow through the layers, each applying weights, biases and an activation function, producing a prediction at the output.
We measure how wrong the prediction is with a loss function - mean squared error for regression, cross-entropy for classification.
Backpropagation is just the chain rule applied systematically: we compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, layer by layer, moving backwards from the output.
The learning rate controls the step size. Set it too high and training overshoots and diverges; too low and learning crawls. It is the single most important hyperparameter to tune.
Plain stochastic gradient descent works, but momentum smooths the updates, and Adam adapts the learning rate per parameter - which is why Adam is the default optimizer almost everywhere.
Convolutional neural networks are the workhorse of computer vision. Let's build the intuition from scratch.
A convolution slides a small filter - say three by three - across the image, multiplying and summing at each position. Each filter produces a feature map.
Early layers learn to detect edges and simple textures; deeper layers combine them into shapes, parts, and eventually whole objects.
Max pooling downsamples each feature map by keeping only the strongest activation in each window, making the representation smaller and more translation-invariant.
Stride controls how far the filter jumps each step, and padding adds a border of zeros so the output keeps the same spatial size.
After several convolution and pooling stages, a small fully connected head turns the final feature maps into class scores.
A practical tip: data augmentation - random crops, flips and color jitter - is the cheapest way to make a CNN generalize better.

videos.title: RNNs and LSTMs: Sequence Modeling Basics

chunks.text: Text, speech and time series arrive one step at a time. Recurrent neural networks were built for exactly that.
An RNN reads a sequence element by element, carrying a hidden state forward - a running summary of everything seen so far.
The catch is the vanishing gradient problem: as gradients are multiplied backwards through many time steps they shrink towards zero, so plain RNNs forget long-range dependencies.
LSTMs fix this with three gates - a forget gate, an input gate and an output gate - that learn what to erase, what to store and what to reveal at each step.
The cell state acts like a conveyor belt running through time, letting information travel long distances almost unchanged.
GRUs simplify the design to two gates and often match LSTM accuracy while training faster.
Before transformers took over, LSTMs powered speech recognition, machine translation and predictive text on your phone.

videos.title: Transformers Explained: Attention Is All You Need

chunks.text: In 2017 the paper 'Attention Is All You Need' by Vaswani and colleagues removed recurrence entirely and replaced it with attention. This is the transformer.

Self-attention works with three vectors per token: a query, a key and a value. Each token's query is compared with every other token's key, and the resulting scores decide how much of each value to blend in.
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, letting different heads specialize - one might track syntax while another tracks coreference.
Because attention itself ignores word order, transformers add positional encodings - sine and cosine waves of different frequencies - so the model knows where each token sits.
The original architecture stacks an encoder that reads the input and a decoder that generates the output, connected by cross-attention.
The killer advantage over RNNs is parallelism: every token is processed at once instead of one step at a time, which is what made training on massive datasets practical.
GPT keeps only the decoder, BERT keeps only the encoder - virtually every modern language model is a descendant of this one architecture.
How can a computer know that 'car' and 'automobile' mean the same thing? The answer is embeddings.
An embedding model maps text into a high-dimensional vector such that semantically similar texts land close together in that space.
Closeness is usually measured with cosine similarity - the angle between two vectors - which ignores their length and focuses on direction.
Semantic search embeds your query and finds the nearest stored vectors, so it matches meaning: a search for 'how to fix a flat tire' finds 'repairing a punctured wheel'.
Vector databases like pgvector or dedicated engines index millions of embeddings for fast approximate nearest neighbor lookup.

Retrieval augmented generation, or RAG, bolts this onto an LLM: retrieve the most relevant chunks for a question, put them in the prompt, and the model answers grounded in your documents instead of hallucinating.
The most underrated knob in a RAG system is chunking: chunks that are too big dilute the signal, too small lose context. Tune it before anything else.

videos.title: GANs: How Machines Learn to Create

chunks.text: Generative adversarial networks taught machines to create images that never existed. Here's how the trick works.
A GAN is two networks locked in a game: a generator that fabricates samples from random noise, and a discriminator that tries to tell fakes from real data.
Think of a counterfeiter and a detective: the counterfeiter improves until the detective can no longer tell the difference. That equilibrium is the training goal.
The most famous failure mode is mode collapse: the generator finds one image that reliably fools the discriminator and produces it over and over, instead of covering the whole diversity of the data.
Training is notoriously unstable - tricks like feature matching, label smoothing and careful learning-rate balance between the two networks are essential in practice.
DCGAN established the convolutional recipe that made GANs work on images, and StyleGAN later produced photorealistic faces of people who do not exist.
Reinforcement learning is learning by trial and error: an agent acts in an environment and receives rewards that tell it how well it is doing.

The core dilemma is exploration versus exploitation: keep choosing the action that has worked best so far, or try something new that might be better? Epsilon-greedy handles this by acting randomly a small fraction of the time.
Q-learning maintains a table of values - the expected future reward for each action in each state - updated with the Bellman equation after every step.
Deep Q-networks replaced the table with a neural network, and in 2015 DeepMind used one to reach superhuman play on dozens of Atari games straight from pixels.
Policy gradient methods skip values entirely and directly adjust the policy - the probability of each action - in the direction that increases reward.
PPO, proximal policy optimization, is today's default: it clips each policy update so no single step can change behavior too drastically, trading a little speed for a lot of stability.
The same recipe - a reward signal plus PPO - is what fine-tunes chatbots from human feedback, a topic we touch on in our fine-tuning video.

videos.title: AI Ethics: Bias in Machine Learning

chunks.text: A model is only as fair as the data and choices behind it. Today we look at where bias in machine learning actually comes from.
Bias usually enters through training data: if a hiring dataset reflects decades of skewed decisions, a model trained on it will faithfully reproduce that skew.

A landmark study found commercial facial recognition systems misclassified darker-skinned women at dramatically higher rates than lighter-skinned men - a direct consequence of unrepresentative training sets.

Fairness can be measured: demographic parity asks whether positive outcomes are distributed equally across groups, while equalized odds asks whether error rates are equal. The two often cannot be satisfied at once.
Documentation helps: datasheets for datasets and model cards force teams to state what data was used, what it covers, and where the model should not be applied.
Regulation is arriving - the EU AI Act classifies systems by risk and puts hard obligations on high-risk uses like hiring and credit scoring.
Our practical checklist: audit your data before training, measure error rates per subgroup, document limitations, and keep a human in the loop for consequential decisions.
You don't need a datacenter to specialize a large language model. This video is about fine-tuning on a budget.
Full fine-tuning updates every weight of the model and needs the memory to match - for a 70B model that means multiple high-end GPUs before you train a single step.

LoRA - low-rank adaptation - freezes the base model and trains only tiny low-rank adapter matrices inserted into each layer. You typically touch well under one percent of the parameters and can merge the adapter back in afterwards.
QLoRA goes further: quantize the frozen base model to four bits, then train LoRA adapters on top. A single consumer GPU can fine-tune a model that would otherwise need a cluster.
Data beats scale here: a few thousand clean, well-formatted, task-specific examples routinely outperform millions of noisy scraped ones.
Always hold out an evaluation set and watch it during training - on small datasets an LLM can memorize the training examples in a couple of epochs, and the eval curve is how you catch it.
Recipe recap: pick a strong small base model, QLoRA on clean data, evaluate on held-out prompts, and stop early. That's the whole budget playbook.
